opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most important questions right now. Training a single giant model from scratch costs an enormous amount, and that's very hard for academic labs or open-source communities to match. But I don't think the answer is to compete directly on scale. There are a few directions I'm excited about.

One is compositionality. A lot of my own work looks at how to build generative systems by composing multiple smaller models instead of training one monolithic model. If you have one model that understands objects, another that understands lighting or physics, and another for language, you can combine them at inference time, for example by adding their energy functions or scores, to generate things none of them saw during training. That's much cheaper, because each piece can be trained separately, often by different groups, and then reused. It's a bit like open-source software, where people build libraries that others plug together.

A second direction is using existing pretrained models better. Once a strong base model exists, especially an open one, you can do a lot with fine-tuning, adapters, or prompting it inside a larger system. You can treat these models as priors and build planning, reasoning, or robotics systems on top of them without paying the pretraining cost again.

Third, there's a lot of room for algorithmic efficiency. Diffusion models used to need hundreds of sampling steps, and now we can get good results in a handful. Better architectures, better data curation, and smarter training objectives can each cut compute by large factors. Historically, those gains have often mattered more than raw hardware.

And finally, there's collaboration: distributed training across institutions, shared datasets and checkpoints, and public compute initiatives. No single university can afford a frontier-scale cluster, but a community pooling resources and sharing modular components can get surprisingly far.

So my view is that open source probably won't win by building the biggest model. It can win by building systems that are more modular, more reusable, and more efficient, and in the long run that may also be the better way to get generalization.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions public compute initiatives and pooled collaboration, but does not suggest a publicly funded research effort on the scale of the Large Hadron Collider.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and I think it's something a lot of us in academia think about constantly, because we just don't have the same compute budgets as the big labs.

My honest take is that the answer isn't really to try to match them on raw scale. Training a frontier model from scratch costs hundreds of millions of dollars, and I don't think the open-source community is going to win by just throwing GPUs at the problem. Where I think there's real leverage is in being smarter about how we use compute.

One direction I'm pretty excited about is compositionality. Instead of training one gigantic monolithic model that has to know everything, you train many smaller models, each of which captures some piece of the world, and then you combine them at inference time. In my own work on compositional generative models, we've shown that you can take separately trained diffusion models, say one that understands one concept and one that understands another, and compose them together to generate things that neither model saw during training. Each of those components can be trained on a single GPU, or a handful of GPUs, by a grad student. And the nice thing is that once they exist, anyone can mix and match them. That feels very much in the spirit of open source: lots of people contributing small pieces that add up to something larger.

The second thing is that I think we've underinvested in inference-time computation. Right now most of the cost goes into training, and then at test time the model just does a single forward pass. But if you think about how people solve hard problems, we spend more time thinking when the problem is harder. Energy-based models, iterative refinement, search, verification, these are all ways of trading extra compute at inference for a smaller, cheaper base model. A smaller model that can reason iteratively can often match a much larger model that can't, and that's a trade that's much more favorable for people who don't own a data center.

And then the third piece, which is maybe less glamorous, is just that open-source lets us share the expensive artifacts. Once someone has paid the cost to train a good base model and releases it, everyone downstream gets to fine-tune or adapt it for a tiny fraction of the cost. Things like LoRA and quantization have made it so that you can adapt a pretty capable model on consumer hardware. So the cost is amortized across the whole community rather than being paid over and over.

So I'd say: don't compete on scale, compete on structure. Build models out of modular pieces, let them think longer at inference, and share what's expensive. I'm actually fairly optimistic that over the next few years the gap will narrow, not because open-source gets more GPUs, but because we get better at not needing them.

r001.rationale: The response proposes modular models, inference-time computation, and sharing expensive artifacts; it does not suggest an LHC-scale publicly funded research effort.

astra-6.text:
I think one promising direction is to make it possible for people to contribute smaller models that we can then combine. Right now, the dominant approach is to train one very large model, and that requires a lot of GPUs in one place. That’s difficult for an individual researcher or a small group to do.

But imagine if different groups could train models on different kinds of data, or specialize in different capabilities, and then we had a way to compose those models into a more capable system. You could spread the cost across a community, and people could build on existing contributions instead of retraining everything from scratch.

The challenge is making that composition work efficiently. Combining models can also increase the cost of running them, so it isn’t automatically a solution. But I think it’s an interesting path toward making development more distributed and accessible.

r001.rationale: The candidate proposes distributing development across groups that contribute and combine smaller models. It does not suggest a publicly funded research effort on the scale of the Large Hadron Collider.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one promising direction is to make these models more modular. Right now, the assumption is often that you need to train one enormous model that does everything, and that requires a huge amount of centralized compute. But if you can train smaller models that each capture different capabilities, and then compose them, you could spread that cost across a community.

Different groups could contribute models trained on different types of data or for different tasks, and other people could reuse those components without retraining everything from scratch. There are still research challenges in making that composition work reliably, and it doesn’t eliminate the cost of inference. But it could lower the barrier to contributing and make progress less dependent on having access to a very large GPU cluster.

r001.rationale: The response proposes community-contributed modular models to reduce reliance on large GPU clusters, but does not suggest a publicly funded research effort on the scale of the Large Hadron Collider.
